The inclusion criteria were that all participants must: (a) be aged between 18-22 years, (b) own a smartphone with an Android operating system version 6.0 or later, which is used at least once every day, and not use any other phone, and (c) have no past or current diagnoses of any motor disorders, or symptoms such as tremors, jerks, twitches, spasms or contractions.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

marginal.title: Marginal Significance
marginal.summary_text: You described 2 effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'.

table.text: Excluding the eight inattentive participants resulted in no change, except a marginally significant negative relationship between time spent and anxiety (GAD-7) (PHQ8: β = -0.088 [SE = 0.120], p = 0.465, BF10 = 0.308; GAD7: β = -0.253 [SE = 0.116], p = 0.033, BF10 = 1.789; OCI-R: β = -0.111 [SE = 0.120], p = 0.356, BF10 = 0.354).
table.header: Exploratory dataset

table.text: In summary, there was no evidence that mental health related to objective mean time spent on one's phone per day in the exploratory dataset, apart from a marginally significant negative relationship between anxiety and mean time spent after excluding the eight inattentive participants.

stat_check.summary_text: We detected no errors in t-tests or F-tests.

table.text: We found that, compared with the self-reported Most Automatic App, the self-reported Least Automatic App had a lower SRHI questionnaire score (paired t-test: t(81) = 13.189, p < 0.001, BF10 = 6.315 x 10 18 ) (Figure 4a); as well as a lower average length of time spent in an 'Appsession' (i.e., duration on App in one go before leaving) (paired t-test: t(60) = 2.306, p = 0.025, BF10 = 1.618) (Figure 4b); and was used at least once in a lower proportion of phone sessions (paired t-test: t(76) = 5.937, p < 0.001, BF10 = 159,381.300) (Figure 4c).

table.formatted: Annotations represent significance of paired t-tests comparing the Most Automatic and Least Automatic App scores, with significance levels denoted as follows: * = p < 0.05, ** = p < 0.01, *** = p < 0.001, ns = not significant. (a) The Most Automatic App had a higher in-strength (t(60) = 5.134, p < 0.001, BF10 = 5,233.373), but there was no significant difference in out-strength (t(60) = -1.299, p = 0.199, BF10 = 0.311). (b) The Most Automatic App had a higher in-diversity (t(60) = 4.666, p < 0.001, BF10 = 1,074.696) but a lower out-diversity (t(60) = -3.303, p = 0.002, BF10 = 17.358). (c) The Most Automatic App had higher centrality across two separate operationalizations of node centrality: eigenvector centrality (t(60) = 5.375, p < 0.001, BF10 = 12,091.24) and coreness (t(60) = 4.365, p < 0.001, BF10 = 402.814). (d) Compared to the Most Automatic App, the Least Automatic App had a higher local clustering coefficient (paired ttest: t(60) = -4.915, p < 0.001, BF10 = 2,471.122), but a lower betweenness coefficient (paired ttest: t(60) = 3.907, p < 0.001, BF10 = 97.016).

(a) The Most Automatic App had a higher in-strength (t(60) = 5.134, p < 0.001, BF10 = 5,233.373), but there was no significant difference in out-strength (t(60) = -1.299, p = 0.199, BF10 = 0.311). (b) The Most Automatic App had a higher in-diversity (t(60) = 4.666, p < 0.001, BF10 = 1,074.696) but a lower out-diversity (t(60) = -3.303, p = 0.002, BF10 = 17.358). (c) The Most Automatic App had higher centrality across two separate operationalizations of node centrality: eigenvector centrality (t(60) = 5.375, p < 0.001, BF10 = 12,091.24) and coreness (t(60) = 4.365, p < 0.001, BF10 = 402.814). (d) Compared to the Most Automatic App, the Least Automatic App had a higher local clustering coefficient (paired ttest: t(60) = -4.915, p < 0.001, BF10 = 2,471.122), but a lower betweenness coefficient (paired ttest: t(60) = 3.907, p < 0.001, BF10 = 97.016).

table.formatted: Annotations represent significance of paired t-tests comparing the Most Automatic and Least Automatic App scores, with significance levels denoted as follows: * = p < 0.05, ** = p < 0.01, *** = p < 0.001, ns = not significant. (a) The Most Automatic App had a higher in-strength (t(60) = 5.134, p < 0.001, BF10 = 5,233.373), but there was no significant difference in out-strength (t(60) = -1.299, p = 0.199, BF10 = 0.311). (b) The Most Automatic App had a higher in-diversity (t(60) = 4.666, p < 0.001, BF10 = 1,074.696) but a lower out-diversity (t(60) = -3.303, p = 0.002, BF10 = 17.358). (c) The Most Automatic App had higher centrality across two separate operationalizations of node centrality: eigenvector centrality (t(60) = 5.375, p < 0.001, BF10 = 12,091.24) and coreness (t(60) = 4.365, p < 0.001, BF10 = 402.814). (d) Compared to the Most Automatic App, the Least Automatic App had a higher local clustering coefficient (paired ttest: t(60) = -4.915, p < 0.001, BF10 = 2,471.122), but a lower betweenness coefficient (paired ttest: t(60) = 3.907, p < 0.001, BF10 = 97.016).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 46 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: We found that, compared with the self-reported Most Automatic App, the self-reported Least Automatic App had a lower SRHI questionnaire score (paired t-test: t(81) = 13.189, p < 0.001, BF10 = 6.315 x 10 18 ) (Figure 4a); as well as a lower average length of time spent in an 'Appsession' (i.e., duration on App in one go before leaving) (paired t-test: t(60) = 2.306, p = 0.025, BF10 = 1.618) (Figure 4b); and was used at least once in a lower proportion of phone sessions (paired t-test: t(76) = 5.937, p < 0.001, BF10 = 159,381.300) (Figure 4c).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Data collection was approved by the University of Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee (PRE.2023.013).
live_data_statements: However, if participants had interpreted the questions to some extent as intended, we would expect the Most Automatic App to exhibit systematic differences in objective use from the Least Automatic App.

Qualtrics platform to establish that they met all inclusion criteria, then read a study Information Sheet, completed a quiz to establish they had sufficiently understood the study in order to provide informed consent, and finally provided informed consent using a checkbox on Qualtrics.
Participants who provided informed consent were then contacted by email by a researcher from the team to arrange a time for data collection.
After the data collection week, participants had another video call with the researcher.
Finally, after completion, participants were asked, 'We care about the quality of our data.

Further, participants completed measures of attentional control via the short-form Attentional Control Scale (ACS) (35); short-form 10-item version at the Affective Research Core short-form materials (University of Wisconsin-Madison; https://arc.psych.wisc.edu/self-report/attention-control-scale-attc/))) and behavioural inhibition and activation systems (the Behavioural Inhibition / Behavioural Activation Scale (BIS/BAS)) (36).
Lastly, participants completed the Self-Reported Habit Index (SRHI), a twelve-item questionnaire where the self-reported habitual nature of a given activity is reported (37).
Participants completed the SRHI four times, where the activity in question was social media, their phone, and the Apps that they selfreported using most and least automatically.

To establish these 'most automatic' and 'least automatic' apps for each participant, participants were first asked for a free-text response to the questions, 'Which App on your phone do you use in the most automatic way, rather than for a specific, planned purpose?' and 'Which App on your phone do you use in the least automatic way, and mostly just for a specific, planned purpose?'

We had also installed a 'pause' button in the Data Collection App so that participants were able to pause data collection whenever they wanted. 34 participants used the 'pause' button at least once during the data collection week.
Participants were aged between 15.7 to 18.3 years at the time of responding to the YSR, which took place before the EARS App was downloaded.
Before pre-processing, participants had EARS App data for mean 21.90 days (minimum = 1, maximum = 25, SD = 4.50).

Participants were recruited via a variety of methods including via social media, the University of Cambridge MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit participant SONA panel, on-campus advertisements, and word of mouth.

The inclusion criteria were that all participants must: (a) be aged between 18-22 years, (b) own a smartphone with an Android operating system version 6.0 or later, which is used at least once every day, and not use any other phone, and (c) have no past or current diagnoses of any motor disorders, or symptoms such as tremors, jerks, twitches, spasms or contractions.
All participants were compensated £55 for completing the study.

We used passively collected smartphone-use data from the ABCD Effortless Assessment Research System (EARS; Ksana Health) (39) and corresponding mental-health measures from the ABCD database at the Session-7A assessment, collected when participants were aged 15-18 between 2024-2025.

text.text: Despite substantial concern about how technology use relates to mental health, research attempting to identify beneficial or harmful smartphone activities has yielded mixed results.
Here, we show that abstracting away from specific activities, their transition patterns across time relate robustly to user mental health.
To quantify this transition structure, we develop a novel network analysis method to capture how each phone user journeys across Apps within a smartphone session.

Across two independent datasets, including an exploratory UK sample aged 18-22 (n = 82), and a preregistered replication in the USA aged 15-18 (n = 565, ABCD cohort), we show that 'App-journey' networks relate consistently to user mental health.

For example, users with higher anxiety symptoms transition to a wider variety of Apps within each phone session (higher network density) and are less likely to confine each session to repeated groups of Apps (lower network modularity).
In contrast, we find no relationship between ADHD and network modularity or density, suggesting that App-journey networks may distinguish among different mental health profiles.
Additionally, in the exploratory dataset, Apps which users describe as more 'automatic' are more central in App-journey networks.
In summary, we uncover a relationship between the temporal structure of digital activity and specific mental health symptom categories, which generalizes across samples and age groups.
The temporal structure of digital activity may thus represent a hitherto neglected, potentially clinically-relevant dimension of digital behaviour for future research and interventions.
There is considerable concern about the impact of excessive smartphone use on young people's mental health (1) (2) (3)).
text.formatted: There is considerable concern about the impact of excessive smartphone use on young people's mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>).

text.text: Yet research relating mental health to time spent on one's phone, and even to specific phone activities, has uncovered inconsistent associations, ranging from positive, to negative or no relationship (4-7).

One possibility is that smartphone activities which may not be individually problematic could become harmful in the context of phone use because of the way that users transition between these activities.
While phones offer new opportunities to communicate with friends, learn information and more, they also intermix these activities in the same device and format in unique ways.
As such, the structure of how digital activities interact may itself generate benefits and harms that cannot be inferred from studying single activities in isolation.
The patterns of inter-relationship between different phone activities within a session could plausibly be both a consequence and a cause of poor mental health.
When phone sessions deviate from original intentions, or begin with no specific goal, they are more likely to lead to regret (8, 9).
text.formatted: When phone sessions deviate from original intentions, or begin with no specific goal, they are more likely to lead to regret <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9)</ref>.

text.text: For example, spending time messaging a friend can cause subsequent regret if one had originally opened the phone just to use the calculator, but might not cause regret if one had opened the phone with the purpose to communicate (10).
text.formatted: For example, spending time messaging a friend can cause subsequent regret if one had originally opened the phone just to use the calculator, but might not cause regret if one had opened the phone with the purpose to communicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Given that regret is associated with negative mood (11), smartphone use featuring higher interference between different activities could lead to poorer mental health, marked by cycles of negative mood or depressive symptoms (9).
text.formatted: Given that regret is associated with negative mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(11)</ref>, smartphone use featuring higher interference between different activities could lead to poorer mental health, marked by cycles of negative mood or depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, depression and anxiety are often comorbid with reduced concentration and attentional control, which could increase the risk of distraction during phone use, causing greater interference between different phone activities (12) (13) (14).
text.formatted: Conversely, depression and anxiety are often comorbid with reduced concentration and attentional control, which could increase the risk of distraction during phone use, causing greater interference between different phone activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(14)</ref>.

text.text: In this way, the structure of different phone activities across time might relate to mental health via bi-directional causal pathways.
Therefore, this structure could be an informative dimension when understanding the link between smartphone use and mental health.
To our knowledge, most previous studies measuring transitions between smartphone activities have relied on participant self-reports (8, 9, 15).
text.formatted: To our knowledge, most previous studies measuring transitions between smartphone activities have relied on participant self-reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">15)</ref>.

text.text: However, self-report involves high participant burden, introduces potential demand characteristics and also requires sufficient self-awareness for accurate reporting (16, 17).
text.formatted: However, self-report involves high participant burden, introduces potential demand characteristics and also requires sufficient self-awareness for accurate reporting <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">17)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, approaches using objective data often enumerate App transitions without situating them within the wider context of holistic activity journeys, which may carry additional information (18).
text.formatted: Alternatively, approaches using objective data often enumerate App transitions without situating them within the wider context of holistic activity journeys, which may carry additional information <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(18)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, inferring characteristics of smartphone activity journeys directly from objective data could be uniquely informative, as well as representing a scalable, generalizable and privacy-preserving method of quantifying a dimension of technology use which may be mechanistically related to mental health.

In this study, we develop a novel approach to quantify holistic transition patterns among different digital activities, and apply this to exploring the journeys between different Apps within a phone session.
Using objective phone data, we construct networks representing the journeys each phone user takes across different Apps within a phone session, which we term 'App-journey' networks.

As shown in Figure 1, in an 'App-journey' network, all Apps used by that phone user are network nodes, and the connection from one App to another represents the probability that if the phone user uses the former App in a session, they will subsequently use the latter App before ending their session (i.e., locking their phone) (Figure 1).
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, in an 'App-journey' network, all Apps used by that phone user are network nodes, and the connection from one App to another represents the probability that if the phone user uses the former App in a session, they will subsequently use the latter App before ending their session (i.e., locking their phone) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We constructed App-journey networks in two separate datasets, including an exploratory dataset (n = 82, UK-based, aged 18-22, collected by our research team), and a preregistered confirmatory dataset (n = 565, USA-based, aged 15-18, part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) cohort study).
The exploratory dataset was collected for this study, while the confirmatory dataset is a secondary data analysis.
In both datasets, phone data was passively recorded for approximately one week, including which Apps users had in the foreground at any time.
Participants additionally completed a battery of mental health and other questionnaires.

The combination of these different datasets allowed us to investigate whether any associations between App-journey network features and mental health generalized across samples varying in country, age and data collection context.
We hypothesized that App-journeys would relate to a phone user's mental health.

For example, the modularity of an App-journey network indexes the extent to which the user's Apps are organised into discrete 'modules', with each phone session predominantly employing a single module rather than journeying across unrelated modules.

This might represent the extent to which someone uses each phone session for an intended activity (for social, work-related, information-gathering, or entertainment) rather than becoming distracted and journeying to other unrelated phone Apps once entering the phone.

To investigate the relationship between App-journeys and mental health, we correlated features of App-journey networks with scores on mental health questionnaires, measuring selfreported levels of anxiety and depression (both datasets), OCD (exploratory dataset) and ADHD (confirmatory dataset).

We set out to answer three research questions, the first and third of which were preregistered in the confirmatory dataset (while the second was only analysed in the exploratory dataset due to data availability).
First, do the global network properties of App-journeys relate to different mental health categories?
Secondly, do the local network properties of specific Apps in these App-journey networks relate to the extent to which these Apps are subjectively experienced as 'automatic'?

Finally, to contextualise our novel method with more traditional methods used to relate phone use to mental health in media effects research (6), we investigated whether time spent on one's phone related to mental health in our samples. (a) Illustrative schema of an App-journey network.
We defined an 'App-journey' network as a directed, weighted network for each participant in which every App in their data was included as a 'node'.
In this illustrative, simplified example, the user would have used six Apps altogether during the data collection period.
The weight of the edge from App A to App B represents the conditional probability that if App A is used in a session, App B will be used after App A before the phone session ends.
This weight can be asymmetrical between Apps.
For example, here the weight of the edge from Maps to Instagram is 0.7, while the weight of the edge from Instagram to Maps is 0.2. (b) Network modularity.

Network modularity represents the extent to which nodes are organized into distinct communities or 'modules', where each module has stronger or many connections between modules and weaker connections between modules. (c) Network density.
Network density represents the number of edges in the network as a proportion of the total possible number of edges in the network.
While modularity relates to the positions of edges, density relates to the quantity of edges.

In this diagram, both networks in Figure 1b have the same density (number of edges and number of possible edges), but different modularity, to demonstrate the dissociation between these two properties.

text.text: We first hypothesized that the way in which different phone activities relate to each other across time within a session might be an important measure of the nature of phone use, that could relate to mental health.
To test this hypothesis, we constructed 'App-journey' networks for each participant (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: To test this hypothesis, we constructed 'App-journey' networks for each participant (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: Each participant's App-journey network was a directed, weighted network in which each App that a participant used across the data collection week featured as a 'node'.

The weight of the edge between the nodes representing App A and App B was the conditional probability that App B would be used at some point after App A in a session before the session ended, given that App A was used in a session.

For example, the weight of the edge from the YouTube App to the Calculator App would represent the proportion of sessions in the participant's data wherein if the YouTube App was used, the Calculator App was used after the YouTube App before the session ended (Figure 1a).

text.text: To address our first research question about whether properties of App-journey networks related to mental health, we extracted global (network-level) network properties and related these to mental health questionnaires in both datasets.
In the exploratory dataset, we additionally related these features to cognitive measures including attentional control, selfreported habit and behavioural inhibition / activation system (BIS/BAS).
The associations between mental health questionnaires were preregistered and tested in the confirmatory dataset and are reported here.

The exploratory results relating all the cognitive questionnaires to App-journey network features, which are all null apart from the association between attentional control and modularity, are reported in the Supplementary Information.
Different mental health questionnaire measures were used in each dataset.
Specifically, in the exploratory dataset we measured depression using the PHQ-8 (19), anxiety using the GAD-7 (20) and OCD using the OCI-R (21).
text.formatted: Specifically, in the exploratory dataset we measured depression using the PHQ-8 (19), anxiety using the GAD-7 (20) and OCD using the OCI-R <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(21)</ref>.

text.text: We then preregistered (22) that we would conduct linear regression models using App-journey network modularity and density to predict depression, anxiety and ADHD in the confirmatory dataset, each measured using the Youth Self-Report Diagnostic Statistical Manual (YSR DSM)-oriented subscales (23).
text.formatted: We then preregistered (22) that we would conduct linear regression models using App-journey network modularity and density to predict depression, anxiety and ADHD in the confirmatory dataset, each measured using the Youth Self-Report Diagnostic Statistical Manual (YSR DSM)-oriented subscales <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(23)</ref>.

text.text: Although we only preregistered to test the direct relationship between each mental health questionnaire score and App-journey network features, we also conducted exploratory analyses testing robustness to several controls.

These controls were the following: mean time spent per day on the phone; overall number of Apps in each participant's network; and removal of participant outliers with scores above 1.5 times the interquartile range away from the upper or lower quartile (see Methods for further details including numbers of outliers excluded for each variable).
In the exploratory dataset, we additionally tested robustness to removal of the eight participants who failed one or more of the quality and attention checks during questionnaire completion.

To test for these relationships, we used App-journey network features to predict scores on questionnaires, in single or multiple linear regression models for uncontrolled or controlled relationships, respectively.
All results for these exploratory sensitivity analyses are reported for the exploratory dataset in Table 1, and for the confirmatory dataset in Table 2.

text.text: We report statistical results for each dataset, which are exploratory for the UK dataset (n = 82) and confirmatory after preregistration for the USA dataset (n = 565).
In each case, we base our interpretations of results on frequentist statistics (p-values) at the α = 0.05 significance level.

However, we also report the results of Bayesian statistics alongside, to quantify the strength of evidence according to the conventional interpretation of Bayes Factors as reported in Lee and Wagenmakers (2013), and we explicitly discuss Bayesian statistics in the results only when interpreting null findings.
Further details on the interpretation of Bayesian statistics can be found in the Methods.

text.text: Network modularity represents the extent to which the network is organized into distinct node 'communities', with higher modularity signifying many or stronger connections within each community and fewer or weaker connections between communities (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: Network modularity represents the extent to which the network is organized into distinct node 'communities', with higher modularity signifying many or stronger connections within each community and fewer or weaker connections between communities (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: In the context of App-journey networks, higher modularity suggests that these communities stay relatively stable across sessions; in other words, the same Apps typically occur together in the same session rather than occurring with different Apps each session.

We found that in the exploratory dataset, network modularity negatively predicted mental health for all three questionnaires; depression (PHQ-8), anxiety (GAD-7) and OCD (OCI-R) (PHQ-8: β = -0.265 [SE = 0.108], p = 0.016, BF10 = 3.015; GAD-7: β = -0.254 [SE = 0.112], p = 0.021, BF10 = 2.428; OCI-R: β = -0.368 [SE = 0.104], p < 0.001, BF10 = 42.060) (Figure 2a, Table 1).

text.text: In the confirmatory dataset, results relating depression and anxiety to modularity replicated in direction from the exploratory dataset (YSR DSM depression: β = -0.118 [SE = 0.042], p = 0.005, BF10 = 4.348; YSR DSM anxiety: β = -0.121 [SE = 0.042], p = 0.004, BF10 = 5.506).

However, in contrast to depression and anxiety, there was no significant relationship between modularity and ADHD, with substantial evidence for the null hypothesis of no relationship (YSR DSM ADHD: β = -0.035 [SE = 0.042], p = 0.410, BF10 = 0.131).
Overall, relating App-journey network modularity to mental health reveals that young people with lower levels of depression and anxiety symptoms exhibit more modular App-journeys.

Modularity also related to OCD symptoms in the exploratory dataset (we did not test OCD in the confirmatory dataset), but in the confirmatory dataset we found evidence against a relationship between modularity and ADHD symptoms.

In other words, adolescents with lower levels of depression and anxiety typically use their smartphone Apps in more distinct communities, wherein community membership is consistent across phone sessions, and are also less likely to transition from one group of Apps to another group within a given phone session.
However, this relationship may be specific to certain mental health profiles, as it does not extend to ADHD.

text.text: We next related App-journey network density to questionnaire scores (Figure 2b).
text.formatted: We next related App-journey network density to questionnaire scores (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>).

text.text: Network density is the proportion of actual edges in a network relative to the number of possible edges (Figure 1c).
text.formatted: Network density is the proportion of actual edges in a network relative to the number of possible edges (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>).

text.text: This can be understood as the extent to which phone users journey randomly across many Apps in each phone session, rather than taking the same journey across fewer Apps each time.

In the exploratory dataset, App-journey network density was significantly positively related to mental health symptoms, with denser App-journey networks predicting higher symptoms of depression, anxiety and OCD (PHQ-8: β = 0.

In contrast, in the confirmatory dataset, of the analysed mental health questionnaires, only anxiety showed a significant positive relationship with App-journey network density (replicating the direction in the exploratory dataset) (YSR DSM Anxiety: β = 0.088 [SE = 0.042], p = 0.037, BF10 = 0.792).

In contrast, Bayes Factors showed there was substantial evidence for the null hypothesis of no relationship with depression (YSR DSM Depression: β = 0.061 [SE = 0.042], p = 0.004, BF10 = 0.260), and ADHD (YSR DSM ADHD: β = -0.036 [SE = 0.042], p = 0.392, BF10 = 0.134).

Overall, relating App-journey network density to mental health reveals that young people with higher anxiety symptoms exhibit denser App-journeys, but not those with higher depression or ADHD symptoms.
Density also related to OCD symptoms in the exploratory dataset (we did not test OCD in the confirmatory dataset).
This suggests that those with higher levels of anxiety journey to a wider variety of Apps within a session, with App connections less consistent across sessions.

In summary, we investigated how the global App-journey network features modularity and density predicted mental health symptoms, and found similar relationships across both datasets among internalizing mental health categories, although a different relationship for externalizing ADHD.

Increased anxiety symptoms were associated with lower App-journey network modularity and higher App-journey network density, while increased depressive symptoms were associated with higher network modularity in both datasets.

In the exploratory dataset, OCD followed the same associations as anxiety and depression, being negatively associated with modularity and positively associated with density; this data was not collected in the confirmatory dataset.
In the confirmatory dataset, ADHD symptoms showed no relationship with either App-journey network feature.
This suggests that the transition patterns across different phone Apps relate to mental health, robustly across samples varying in country and age.

For Most and Least automatic Apps, the 10 unique App names with the highest frequencies are shown in separate bars, and all further answers are grouped under 'Other'.
Our next research question concerned whether the self-reported most and least 'automatic' Apps played different roles in App-journey networks.
These self-reports, and all associated analyses, are only available in the exploratory dataset and were therefore not preregistered.

During data collection, we asked each participant to report the two Apps which they considered that they used most and least automatically, and we henceforth refer to their answers to this as their Most and Least Automatic Apps, respectively.
Please see Methods for the exact wording of these questions.

Participants then completed the Self-Reported Habit Index (SRHI) questionnaire for their answers to both the Most Automatic and Least Automatic App separately, to index their subjective habit strength for these two different Apps.
Participants also completed the SRHI questionnaire two further times, for social media and their phone (i.e., to indicate how habitually they used social media and their phones, respectively).
Figure 3 summarizes the specific App names and categories reported as the Most and Least Automatic Apps.

text.text: In our sample,

Instagram was the most commonly reported Most Automatic App (38 out of 80 responses), while social media was the most popular category among Most Automatic Apps (55 out of 80 Apps), with other social media Apps reported including TikTok (n = 7), Twitter/X (n = 7) and Facebook (n = 3).

In contrast, Google Maps was the most popular App chosen as the Least Automatic App (8 out of 80 responses), while 'Directions, schedule, weather and journey planning' was the most popular category for Least Automatic App (10 out of 80 Apps).

We do not interpret self-reported Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps as necessarily representing the objective most automatic or least automatic apps, as self-reports rely on participants' subjective experiences, memory and interpretation.

However, if participants had interpreted the questions to some extent as intended, we would expect the Most Automatic App to exhibit systematic differences in objective use from the Least Automatic App.

Therefore, as a sanity check to establish whether participants answered the question meaningfully, we examined properties of the Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps in both subjective questionnaire and the objective passively collected Data Collection App data.

We found that, compared with the self-reported Most Automatic App, the self-reported Least Automatic App had a lower SRHI questionnaire score (paired t-test: t(81) = 13.189, p < 0.001, BF10 = 6.315 x 10 18 ) (Figure 4a); as well as a lower average length of time spent in an 'Appsession' (i.e., duration on App in one go before leaving) (paired t-test: t(60) = 2.306, p = 0.025, BF10 = 1.618) (Figure 4b); and was used at least once in a lower proportion of phone sessions (paired t-test: t(76) = 5.937, p < 0.001, BF10 = 159,381.300) (Figure 4c).

text.text: We next wanted to understand whether the location or role of specific Apps within Appjourney networks related to the likelihood that that App was subjectively experienced as 'automatic'.
To this end, we compared local (node-level) network properties between the Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps.
In all, we compared node in-strength and out-strength, in-diversity and out-diversity, centrality, local clustering and betweenness, to gain a comprehensive understanding of node positions.
We first compared node strength, which is the sum of weights of all edges connected to a node (Figure 5a).
text.formatted: We first compared node strength, which is the sum of weights of all edges connected to a node (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">5a</ref>).

text.text: This can be separated into 'in-strength' and 'out-strength', which are the sum of all in-weights and out-weights, respectively.

Given that 'in-strength' represents the sum of the conditional probabilities that the App in question would be visited after any other App, a higher in-strength captures the intuition that there is a high probability of ending up on the App in question after visiting other Apps.
In contrast, 'out-strength' represents the probability of transitioning to any other App after using the App in question (at any point in the same session), as opposed to simply ending the session.
A higher 'out-strength' suggests that a phone user typically continues to more Apps after using the App in question (rather than just locking the phone immediately).

text.text: Next, we compared node diversity, which quantifies how evenly a node's weights are distributed across other nodes, using Shannon's entropy (25) (Figure 5b).

text.text: Like network strength measures, diversity can be divided into in-diversity and out-diversity.

In-diversity describes the entropy across other Apps from which the user might transition to an App in question, with higher in-diversity suggesting the user typically visits a more even distribution of Apps before using the App in each session.
High out-diversity suggests that a more evenly distributed variety of Apps are visited after the App in question before ending the session.
Compared with the Least Automatic App, the Most Automatic App had higher in-diversity (t(60) = 4.666, p < 0.001, BF10 = 1,074.696) but lower out-diversity (t(60) = -3.303, p = 0.002, BF10 = 17.358).

text.text: This suggests that the user would transition from a more evenly-distributed range of Apps to the Most Automatic App during a session than to the Least Automatic App.
However, after using the Most Automatic App, there was a less evenly distributed range of Apps which would be visited before turning off the phone compared with the Least Automatic app.
We then compared node centrality between Most Automatic and Least Automatic apps (Figure 5c).
text.formatted: We then compared node centrality between Most Automatic and Least Automatic apps (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">5c</ref>).

text.text: Centrality conceptually indexes the importance or influence of a node in the network.
This concept builds on node-level properties like strength and diversity by considering also the node-level properties of other nodes in the network.
Alternative measures of centrality can be distinguished by the different ways in which they weight constituent features.
For example, 'eigenvector centrality' assigns relative scores to all nodes, with connections to other high-scoring nodes increasing each node's score.

In contrast, 'coreness' is a measure of how centrally-embedded a node is within the network, such that nodes with high coreness are deeply embedded within the network's structure, by being connected to a higher number of subgroups.
We compared both eigenvector centrality and coreness between Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps.

Across participants, the Most Automatic App had both a higher eigenvector centrality (paired t-test: t(60) = 5.375, p < 0.001, BF10 = 12,091.24) and higher coreness (t(60) = 4.365, p < 0.001, BF10 = 402.814).

text.text: In summary, across two measures of centrality, the Most Automatic App was more central in App-journey networks than the Least Automatic App.
This is consistent with the interpretation that regardless of a user's original purpose for opening their phone, they will still more typically end up using the Most Automatic App.
Finally, we compared the local clustering coefficient and betweenness between the Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps (Figure 5d).
text.formatted: Finally, we compared the local clustering coefficient and betweenness between the Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">5d</ref>).

text.text: The local clustering coefficient quantifies the extent to which a node's neighbours are also interconnected with one another.

We computed this using a weighted generalisation of the clustering coefficient, applied to the undirected version of the network, where edge weights reflected connection strength (i.e., stronger connections corresponded to higher weights).
This measure therefore captures the degree of local "triadic closure" around each node, taking into account both the presence and strength of connections between neighbouring nodes.

In contrast, betweenness quantifies the extent to which a node lies on the shortest paths between all other pairs of nodes in the network and can therefore be interpreted as an index of how frequently a node acts as a bridge between distinct node communities.
We computed betweenness centrality on the directed weighted network, using edge weights reflecting connection strength, such that stronger connections contributed to shorter path lengths.
Local clustering coefficient and betweenness centrality capture complementary aspects of network organisation.
The local clustering coefficient indexes the tendency for a node's immediate neighbours to be densely interconnected, reflecting locally cohesive or "clustered" neighbourhood structure.
In contrast, betweenness centrality captures the extent to which a node connects different parts of the network, reflecting a more global bridging or brokerage role.

Accordingly, nodes with high clustering tend to be embedded within tightly interconnected local neighbourhoods, whereas nodes with high betweenness tend to link otherwise separate regions of the network.

Compared to the Most Automatic App, we found that the Least Automatic App had a higher Taking these findings regarding local clustering and betweenness together, it seems that the Least Automatic App is more likely to be embedded within a closely clustered module, while the Most Automatic App is more likely to connect across disconnected modules, consistent with the idea that it takes part in more disparate sessions rather than occurring only in certain types of sessions.

Finally, we wanted to understand our novel method of measuring phone behaviour in the context of more conventional methods of relating technology use to mental health (6), by relating objective mean time spent per day to mental health scores.

To preview, we found no relationships between mental health and time spent in the exploratory dataset, but, in a preregistered analysis, found relationships between mental health and time spent for all three mental health questionnaires in the confirmatory dataset (including ADHD, which did not relate to App-journey network features).
Mean time spent on one's phone per day did not significantly predict scores on any mental health questionnaires in the exploratory dataset.

The Bayes Factor analysis indicated substantial evidence for the null hypothesis of no relationship to depression and anxiety, and anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis of no relationship to OCD (PHQ8: β = 0.

In summary, there was no evidence that mental health related to objective mean time spent on one's phone per day in the exploratory dataset, apart from a marginally significant negative relationship between anxiety and mean time spent after excluding the eight inattentive participants.

text.text: In this study, we ask whether the relationship between digital behaviour and mental health depends not just on specific harmful or beneficial activities, but also on how users transition between activities.

We developed a network analysis method to extract properties of each participant's activity journey within a phone session, and related these to mental health across two independent datasets: an exploratory UK sample (n = 82), and a preregistered USA replication (n = 565).

Using this novel approach, we found that the modularity and density of App-journey networks was related to symptoms of anxiety and depression (both datasets), as well as OCD (exploratory only), but not to symptoms of ADHD (confirmatory only).

Furthermore, App-specific analyses in the exploratory dataset revealed that Apps which participants reported using most automatically were more central in App-journey networks than Apps participants reported using least automatically.
Together, these findings suggest that the transition journeys across smartphone activities may have relevance for mental health and experiences of automatic phone use.

This new dimension of smartphone use may prove a fruitful target for future mental health research and digital wellbeing interventions, helping to move media effects research beyond focusing on time spent or specific activities in isolation.
We constructed 'App-journey' networks to quantify how users journey across different smartphone activities (operationalized as Apps) in a phone session.
This approach abstracts from the specific activities engaged with on a phone, and instead focuses on how a user journeys across different activities over time.

This allows us to extract signatures of phone behaviours predictive of mental health and attentional control, which can generalize across samples, as well as potentially be more robust to the constantly changing contents of specific phone activities (26, 27).
text.formatted: This allows us to extract signatures of phone behaviours predictive of mental health and attentional control, which can generalize across samples, as well as potentially be more robust to the constantly changing contents of specific phone activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">27)</ref>.

text.text: We first found that global features of App-journey networks, modularity and density, predicted mental health symptoms.

In the context of App-journey networks, modularity can be interpreted as the extent to which Apps are typically used together in subgroups during a given phone session, as opposed to the user journeying from one subgroup to another within each session.
On the other hand, density describes how many pairs of Apps were used in the same session at least once, as a proportion of possible pairs of Apps that could have been used together.
We found that anxiety related to both modularity and density, while depression related only to modularity.

We additionally examined only OCD in the exploratory dataset, and found that both OCD symptoms were predicted by lower modularity and higher density, following the same pattern as anxiety and depression.

However, preregistered analyses in the confirmatory dataset found no relationship between ADHD symptoms and App-journey network features considered, despite their relationship to objective time spent on one's phone.
We note that this preregistered analysis of ADHD data was not tested in the exploratory dataset.

This dissociation of results between symptoms of internalizing disorders anxiety, depression and OCD, compared with externalizing ADHD, suggests that different mental health profiles may have distinct App-journey networks.
Specifically, phone users with more modular, less dense App-journey networks have lower symptoms of anxiety but there is no evidence for a relationship with ADHD.
Our study was cross-sectional, and therefore there may be several, non-mutually exclusive mechanisms underlying the observed associations between Appjourneys and mental health.

One possibility is that more 'modular' networks represent the extent to which Apps are organized into different 'modules', each representing a different typical phone need -for example, social connection, learning information, work-related activities, and games.

In this context, a more modular and less dense App-journey network might index the extent to which a given user typically uses their phone for a single activitytype per session, rather than deviating from their original intended activity once opening the phone, or having no particular intended activity.
Greater modularity might suggest that an App-journey was more intentional or purposeful.
The psychological literature refers to purpose-oriented behaviour as 'goal-directed' behaviour (28).
text.formatted: The psychological literature refers to purpose-oriented behaviour as 'goal-directed' behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(28)</ref>.

text.text: It might be that smartphone environments, by grouping attractive activities within the same tool, pose a novel challenge for goal commitment when fulfilling these goaldirected uses.
Conversely, and mutually compatibly, less goal-directed phone use could increase regret (8), and inability to stay on task may lower mood with adverse mental health outcomes.
Finally, it is possible that there is no causal relationship between mental health and phone use, and instead that a third factor, such as daily activities, influences them both.

Along with comparing global network features across participants, in the exploratory dataset we additionally analyzed local features of specific nodes (Apps) within these networks which participants reported as using either more or less automatically, within participants.
Participants reported social media as the most popular category for 'Most Automatic' Apps, with the Instagram as the most commonly reported (38 out of 80 responses).
Compared with the 'Least Automatic App', the 'Most Automatic App' had a higher node 'in-strength'.
This suggests that within a phone session, the user is more likely to transition from other Apps to the Most Automatic App than the Least Automatic App.

We also found that the Most Automatic App had a higher in-diversity and lower out-diversity, suggesting that a greater range of Apps transition to it, but that there is a lower range of Apps that it transitions to.
Furthermore, across two measures of centrality, eigenvector centrality and coreness, the Most Automatic App was more central in App-journey networks than the Least Automatic App.

Additionally, the Most Automatic App had lower local clustering and higher betweenness, suggesting it is more likely to connect distinct App communities than the Least Automatic App, which is more likely to be confined within a specific community.
This is consistent with an 'attractive' function wherein phone use with any array of intentions converges more often to using the Most Automatic App.
This pattern likely reflects habitual or more automatic opening of the Most Automatic App (29).
text.formatted: This pattern likely reflects habitual or more automatic opening of the Most Automatic App <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(29)</ref>.

text.text: While behaviors are mostly initiated for the first time by motivational factors like goals or intentions, frequently repeated behaviors can become habitual or automatic (30).
text.formatted: While behaviors are mostly initiated for the first time by motivational factors like goals or intentions, frequently repeated behaviors can become habitual or automatic <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(30)</ref>.

text.text: This means they are performed with less regard for these more conscious motivations and are instead activated upon perception of the context in which they were performed in the past.

In the case of Apps, context cues to habit performance might include notifications, the sight of the App icon on the smartphone screen, or other environmental features and even emotional states or feelings like boredom (24, 31).
text.formatted: In the case of Apps, context cues to habit performance might include notifications, the sight of the App icon on the smartphone screen, or other environmental features and even emotional states or feelings like boredom <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">31)</ref>.

text.text: Given that Most and Least Automatic Apps were identified through self-report, we do not necessarily use these comparisons to index the Most and Least Automatic Apps objectively, but rather to compare automaticity as subjectively experienced by the user.

Sanity checks did ascertain that these self-reports corresponded to objective differences in the relative way in which the two Apps were used, with the Most Automatic App appearing at least once in a higher proportion of sessions and having a typically longer App-session duration.
These findings therefore suggest that the role of an App in an App-journey network is related to the extent to which it is experienced as being used automatically.
In our final preregistered analysis, we attempted to replicate previous literature which has focused on relating mental health to time spent on digital media (6, 32).
text.formatted: In our final preregistered analysis, we attempted to replicate previous literature which has focused on relating mental health to time spent on digital media <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">32)</ref>.

text.text: We found no evidence for an association between objective time spent on the smartphone and mental health in the exploratory dataset, with Bayes Factors suggesting support for the null hypothesis of no relationship.
In contrast, we found a postive relationship between all three mental health questionnaires -anxiety, depression and ADHD -and time spent, in the preregistered confirmatory dataset.
Overall, in this study we have demonstrated that the temporal relationships between different digital activities relates robustly to specific mental health profiles.
Importantly, our study was cross-sectional, meaning that any causal interpretation of relationship between this behaviour and mental health is not yet warranted.

However, this new method of measuring smartphone behaviour paves the way for investigation of causes and effects of different digital journey types, as well as potentially, if a causal relationship is found, informing smartphone interventions.
For example, longitudinal research in future could establish whether increased modularity predicts worsened mental health, or vice versa.

Further, intervention studies could alter mental health states or phone use modularity and examine the effects of this on smartphone behaviour or examine the effects of feedback about smartphone modularity on mental health or behaviour.

If a relationship between App automaticity and network centrality is established, this could also be used to deliver interventions at the App-level which help identify which Apps are most problematic for a given user (33).
text.formatted: If a relationship between App automaticity and network centrality is established, this could also be used to deliver interventions at the App-level which help identify which Apps are most problematic for a given user <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(33)</ref>.

text.text: Properties of App-journey networks are linked to mental health across two independent datasets, including a preregistered replication.

In particular, young people with higher anxiety symptoms exhibit less modular 'App-journey' networks, suggesting lower behavioural organisation across digital activities, although this relationship does not extend to all mental health profiles, with no relationships found between App-journey networks and ADHD.
This novel method of quantitatively characterizing phone behaviour from objective data opens new avenues to identify problematic phone use which go beyond time spent.
In this way, we hope this approach will help to facilitate better understanding of the causal pathways and intervention targets for healthier smartphone use.
We analyzed two datasets: an exploratory dataset of UK-based participants (n = 82), and a confirmatory dataset of USA-based participants (n = 565).
We here describe the data collection, participants and pre-processing details for each dataset in turn, before turning to analysis details for both datasets together.
We note there are several relevant differences in data collection and pre-processing protocols between the two datasets.
For example, App data was recorded before questionnaires in the exploratory dataset, and after in the confirmatory dataset.

Further, App data was limited to exactly the first seven days for every participant in the confirmatory dataset after preprocessing (from an initial collection period of mean 21.7 days), while we used the maximum available number of days in the exploratory dataset which varied across participants (between 3 and 16 days).
Finally, while phone sessions were identified as 'Screen ON' vs.
'OFF' events in the exploratory dataset, in the confirmatory dataset we inferred phone session boundaries during pre-processing as at least five seconds between consecutive App foreground sessions.

Qualtrics platform to establish that they met all inclusion criteria, then read a study Information Sheet, completed a quiz to establish they had sufficiently understood the study in order to provide informed consent, and finally provided informed consent using a checkbox on Qualtrics.
Participants who provided informed consent were then contacted by email by a researcher from the team to arrange a time for data collection.
Our research team developed a novel Data Collection App in order to collect data for this study.

The Data Collection App is downloaded onto a participant's mobile phone, and while downloaded records the following data between when the phone is unlocked and unlocked: the timestamps for when touches (i.e., taps and swipes) occur on the touchscreen, timestamps of unlocking and locking the phone, and the timestamps and names of Apps running in the foreground of the phone.
For ethical reasons to protect participant privacy, the App also included a 'pause' button which, when pressed, would halt all data collection.
Data collection would resume automatically if the pause button was pressed again, or if 60 minutes had passed.
All participants began with an introductory video-call with a member of the research team, where they were introduced to the study and downloaded the App onto their phones.
They were instructed to move the App widget off the immediate homescreen to minimize interference with their normal phone experience routine.

Participants then kept the App recording their data for approximately one week (after excluding first and last partial days, remaining days per participant: minimum = 3 days, maximum = 16 days, median = 8 days, mean = 8.43 days, standard deviation = 1.62 days).
After the data collection week, participants had another video call with the researcher.
During this meeting participants first uninstalled the App from their phones.
They then were sent a link to complete a battery of questionnaires via Qualtrics.
The questionnaires included measures of mental health, behavioural activation and inhibition, attentional control and habits.

To maximize quality of questionnaire answers and minimize likelihood of low-effort or inattentive responding (34), we included quality and attention checks before, during and after questionnaire completion.

The quality checks before completion included the requirements to write two sentences in full English about their favorite book or film at the start, as well as asking participants to commit to providing thoughtful answers at the beginning of the survey, with the question, 'We care about the quality of our survey data.
For us to get the most accurate measures, it is important that you provide thoughtful answers to all questions of this survey.
Do you commit to providing thoughtful answers to the questions in this survey?'
During questionnaire completion, there were three attention checks which consisted of questions in the same format as questionnaire questions but with an obvious correct answer.
These included the questions 'I will often eat rotten food for the enjoyment of it', 'I often spend multiple weeks without eating anything', and 'Please respond with "moderately" to this question.'
Finally, after completion, participants were asked, 'We care about the quality of our data.
To get the most accurate measures, it is important that we only include data that was provided thoughtfully.
Your response to this question will not affect your reimbursement.
Did you provide meaningful/thoughtful answers throughout the survey?'

No participants failed the quality pre-commitment check, two failed the quality postcommitment check, five failed the first attention check, one failed the second attention check and one failed the third attention check.
Only one participant failed more than one of these checks (the first and second attention checks), leaving eight participants in total who failed at least one quality or attention check.

To establish whether these eight participants with potentially low-quality questionnaire answers affected our results, we repeated analyses for all main results with these participants excluded and report all results both with and without these exclusions.
After the data collection week, a researcher met with participants to first download the Data Collection App and then complete nine questionnaires.
This included three mental health questionnaires: the GAD-7 to measure anxiety (20), the PHQ-8 to measure depression (19) and the OCI-R to measure Obsessive Compulsive Disorder tendency (21).

text.text: Participants completed the SRHI four times, where the activity in question was social media, their phone, and the Apps that they selfreported using most and least automatically.

To establish these 'most automatic' and 'least automatic' apps for each participant, participants were first asked for a free-text response to the questions, 'Which App on your phone do you use in the most automatic way, rather than for a specific, planned purpose?' and 'Which App on your phone do you use in the least automatic way, and mostly just for a specific, planned purpose?'
Their answers to these questions were used as the objects for the respective SRHIs.
During data pre-processing, we first checked for irregularities in the data.

We defined a 'session' as the time between each phone unlocking and locking, and an 'App-session' as the time for which a single app was in the foreground within a session, such that there could be multiple App-sessions for the same App within a session.
When examining the data for irregularities, we found that 63 of 482,586 app sessions (0.0001%) were over one hour long, while 575 out of 73,550 phone sessions were over one hour long (0.0078%).

Given that these unexpectedly long App-sessions and sessions represented a very small proportion of the data, although it was possible that such long sessions were the results of technical errors in data collection, or participants leaving their phones on while asleep or absent, we chose not to remove any of these App-sessions or sessions during data pre-processing.

We had also installed a 'pause' button in the Data Collection App so that participants were able to pause data collection whenever they wanted. 34 participants used the 'pause' button at least once during the data collection week.

Rather than removing all the data for these participants, for the analyses of App-level data (i.e. network analyses), we removed all sessions containing at least one pause (240 sessions out of 73,550 sessions; 0.003%).

For analyses in which we calculated means per day (such as, in research question 3, mean time spent per day, and other micro-behaviour variables in the clustering analysis), we removed all days containing at least one pause (78 out of 697 days; 0.112%).

For all analyses relating to the participants' self-reported most and least automatic apps to their objective Data Collection App data (i.e. not for the SRHI for these reported apps), we included only those participants for whom we could identify one unique app which occurred at least once in their data.

text.text: The YSR is a self-report questionnaire designed to obtain data directly from children and adolescents aged 11 to 18 about various competencies and behavioural issues.
The YSR consists of two parts, evlauating first skills and competencies, and then 112 items which explore prosocial behaviours and a range of problem behaviours.

For each item, the adolescent respondent must choose 0 when its content is not true or irrelevant, 1 when it is 'Something true or it happens sometimes' and 2 when it is 'very true and happens frequently'.
The YSR is also widely used in clinical practice to help with diagnosis.

The DSM-oriented scales within the YSR, which were analyzed in this study, are specific groupings within the YSR which can be grouped together to correspond to mental health categories from the Diagnostic Statistical Manual.
These have been shown (in boys) construct validity in predicting their corresponding DSM categories, although imperfectly, with high specificity but low sensitivity (40).

text.text: The appusage2_logs dataset contained 586 unique participants, and after pre-processing excluded 21 participants with less than seven full days of data, we used a final dataset of n = 565.
Participants were aged between 15.7 to 18.3 years at the time of responding to the YSR, which took place before the EARS App was downloaded.

The ABCD 7.0 release did not contain self-reported gender, so we instead report sex assigned at birth (a variable taken from the ABCD static variable dataset), which showed that the n = 565 sample contained 327 males and 238 females (i.e. the sample was 58% male).

The time delay from completion of YSR to the beginning of our retained data for EARS App (i.e., after we excluded the first day of data as it was incomplete) ranged from 0 to 73 days (median = 0.74 days; mean = 2.88 days; SD = 7.01 days).
Before pre-processing, participants had EARS App data for mean 21.90 days (minimum = 1, maximum = 25, SD = 4.50).
We pre-processed both the EARS and the YSR data.

For the EARS data, initial pre-processing was carried out by the Ksana health team, before making data available in the ABCD release, removing known errors (e.g., Apps that are known to run for 24 hours; duplicative events) and undergoing further cleaning processes.
From the original raw datasets, we further preprocessed the EARS data for our analysis.

First, as there was no 'Screen on/off' variable to identify session starts and endings, we needed to infer phone usage sessions (i.e. when a phone was turned on and off) from the dataset, as the App-journey network uses this information to construct network edges (as each represents the conditional probability of visiting the subsequent App during the same phone session).

Using the time-stamps of App foreground sessions, we defined the start of a new 'phone session' as when the start time of an app usage session was 5 seconds or more after the end time of the previous app usage session.

As the App usage data was collected for three weeks for each participant per session, we further restricted all participants to only their first full seven days of data (e.g. if the first day of data collection does not include a whole 24 hours but the second does, we included seven days from the second day onwards).
This was to ensure comparability with the previous sample who used approximately one week of phone-session data.

We excluded all participants who had fewer than seven days of data after removing the first and last incomplete days (excluding n = 21 out of n = 586, leaving n = 565 remaining), and retained exactly the first seven days of data for the remaining 565 participants.

As we consistently retained the first seven days of an approximately three-week collection period, this meant that the gap between the last day of App data collection and the date on which the mental health questionnaires were completed ranged from 7 to 81 days (mean = 9.36 days, median = 7 days, SD = 7.06 days).

The R package igraph (version 2.1.4) was used to conduct network analyses (44).
text.formatted: The R package igraph (version 2.1.4) was used to conduct network analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(44)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, a network was constructed for each participant wherein all Apps which appeared at least once in their data represented 'nodes', and the weight of the edge between App A and App B was the conditional probability that App B was used after App A in a session, given that App A was used in a session.
This was calculated as the number of times that App B was visited after App A in a session, divided by the number of sessions in which App A appeared at least once.
We defined modularity using the 'Louvain' algorithm in igraph (44).
text.formatted: We defined modularity using the 'Louvain' algorithm in igraph <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(44)</ref>.

text.text: The Louvain algorithm calculates the modularity of undirected graphs, therefore we used the function 'as.undirected' to convert each graph before use.
This function turns a directed graph to an undirected graph by adding the weights of edges in each direction to take the sum of all directed weights as the single undirected weight.
We defined density using the 'edge_density' function.
The node-level properties we measured included in-strength, out-strength, in-diversity, outdiversity, eigenvector centrality and coreness.
In-and out-strength were calculated using the function 'strength' in igraph for each node.
In-and out-diversity were calculated by quantifying the Shannon entropy across in-or out-weights, respectively for each node, and were set to 0 in the case where there was just one edge.
Eigenvector centrality and coreness were calculated using the 'eigen_centrality' and 'coreness' igraph functions.

We report both frequentist and Bayesian statistics for all statistical tests investigating our research questions.

We base interpretations in the main paper on frequentist statistics where results were significant, and on Bayesian statistics in the case of null results for frequentist statistical tests, to quantify strength of evidence for each hypothesis even when they are not significant.
In frequentist statistical tests, we treat results as significant if the probability is significant at α = 0.05, two-tailed.
We also provide results of Bayesian hypothesis tests to quantify strength of evidence for each result (45).

Here, we report these analyses in more detail including reporting robustness to exclusions of outliers and exclusion of the eight participants who failed attention checks for questionnaires.
First, analyzing the questionnaire data, we compared SRHI habit scores for the Most Automatic vs.
Least Automatic Apps to each other.
As expected, the Most Automatic App had a significantly higher SRHI habit score than the Least Automatic App (paired t-test: t(81) = 13.189, p < 0.001, BF10 = 6.315 x 10 18 ) (Figure 4a).

text.text: This remained significant with the eight inattentive participants excluded (paired t-test: t(73) = 11.846, p < 0.001, BF10 = 4.756 x 10 15 ).

text.text: In contrast to the Least Automatic App, the Most Automatic App had a significantly higher SRHI than social media (paired t-test: t(81) = -2.755, p = 0.007, BF10 = 4.096), but did not differ significantly from the SRHI for the phone (paired t-test: t(81) = 0.735, p = 0.465, BF10 = 0.158).
Indeed, the BF10 of 0.158 indicates substantial evidence for the null hypothesis that the Most Automatic App did not have a different SRHI score from the phone.
After excluding inattentive participants, no results changed in direction or significance.
The Most Automatic App still had a significantly higher SRHI than social media use (paired t-test: t(73) = -2.459, p = 0.016, BF10 = 2.117).

The relationship between the SRHI for the Most Automatic App and phone use remained nonsignificant, with a BF10 of 0.220 suggesting substantial evidence for the null hypothesis of no difference (paired t-test: t(73) = 1.063, p = 0.292, BF10 = 0.220).
Next, we analyzed the passively collected smartphone data for each participant's Most Automatic and Least Automatic Apps.
For this analysis, we first restricted the sample to those participants for whom we could extract a unique App for both their self-reported Most and Least Automatic Apps (n = 77).

This excluded participants, for example, who reported an App such as 'calculator' but for whom there were two different calculator Apps in their objective data, meaning that we could not uniquely isolate which App they were referring to in the objective data.
Table S1 in the Supplementary Information details how each raw self-reported App answer was converted, if possible, to an App in the objective data.

text.text: We established that compared with the Least Automatic App, the Most Automatic App was used at least once in a higher proportion of phone sessions (paired t-test: t(76) = 5.937, p < 0.001, BF10 = 159,381.300) (Figure 4c).
text.formatted: We established that compared with the Least Automatic App, the Most Automatic App was used at least once in a higher proportion of phone sessions (paired t-test: t(76) = 5.937, p < 0.001, BF10 = 159,381.300) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">4c</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, the mean proportion of sessions containing the Most Automatic App across participants was 0.243, standard deviation 0.180, compared with mean = 0.082, standard deviation = 0.130 for the Least Automatic App.
In other words, a higher proportion of sessions contained the Most Automatic than the Least Automatic App.
We then further restricted the sample to those participants who used both their Most and Least Automatic Apps at least once in their objective data (n = 61).
This would exclude participants for whom, for example, we could identify a unique App for each self-reported Most Automatic or Least Automatic App (e.g.
WhatsApp, Instagram), but who did not use the reported App during the data collection period, and therefore it did not appear in their objective data.

In this subset of participants who used both their Most and Least Automatic Apps at least once (n = 61), we found that the mean length of time each participant spent on the Most Automatic App within each 'App-session' was significantly longer than for the Least Automatic App (paired t-test: t(60) = 2.306, p = 0.025, BF10 = 1.618) (Figure 4b).
text.formatted: In this subset of participants who used both their Most and Least Automatic Apps at least once (n = 61), we found that the mean length of time each participant spent on the Most Automatic App within each 'App-session' was significantly longer than for the Least Automatic App (paired t-test: t(60) = 2.306, p = 0.025, BF10 = 1.618) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">4b</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, the mean of mean durations on the Most Automatic App across participants was 81.237 seconds, standard deviation = 126.838; compared with 35.903 seconds, standard deviation = 71.531 for the Least Automatic App.
Together, these sanity checks confirmed that participants sufficiently understood the concept of automatic App use.
We then investigated, in this n = 61 subset, whether the Most vs.
Least Automatic App was most likely to appear at a specific point in a phone session (Figure 4d).
text.formatted: Least Automatic App was most likely to appear at a specific point in a phone session (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">4d</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, we identified the 'first', 'second', 'penultimate' and 'last' App used in a session (excluding the homescreen; see Materials and Methods and Supplementary Information).
We then compared the probability that each of these four positions would contain the Most Automatic vs.
Least Automatic Apps, across sessions within a participant, and plotted the mean of these probabilities across all participants (Figure 4d).

text.text: Using a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, we found an interaction between position in a session and proportion of times that the Most Automatic vs.

Specifically, there was a significant interaction between position in session (first, second, penultimate or last) and size of difference between proportion of Most Automatic vs.

text.text: Participants were recruited via a variety of methods including via social media, the University of Cambridge MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit participant SONA panel, on-campus advertisements, and word of mouth.
Data collection was approved by the University of Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee (PRE.2023.013).

The inclusion criteria were that all participants must: (a) be aged between 18-22 years, (b) own a smartphone with an Android operating system version 6.0 or later, which is used at least once every day, and not use any other phone, and (c) have no past or current diagnoses of any motor disorders, or symptoms such as tremors, jerks, twitches, spasms or contractions.
All participants were compensated £55 for completing the study.
A total of 104 people participated in the study (i.e., completed objective data collection and filled in the questionnaires at the end of the study).
Exclusions due to malfunctions of the Data Collection App, or failure to complete all questionnaires, yielded a final sample of n = 82 (48 female, 30 male, 4 preferred not to say gender).
Participants who expressed interest completed an initial screening questionnaire on

ABCD) Study, a large, longitudinal study of nearly 12,000 children recruited at ages 9-10 years from 21 research sites across the United States, to investigate brain, cognitive, behavioural, and health development (https://abcdstudy.org) (38).

We used passively collected smartphone-use data from the ABCD Effortless Assessment Research System (EARS; Ksana Health) (39) and corresponding mental-health measures from the ABCD database at the Session-7A assessment, collected when participants were aged 15-18 between 2024-2025.

Although other Sessions (other longitudinal data collection time-points) also included matched mental health and EARS data, Session 7A was chosen as it contained the most participants available with EARS and matched mental health data.

EARS objectively records smartphone application use, including the applications active in the foreground and the corresponding timestamps, providing measures of smartphone activity without requiring participants to self-report their usage.

In the ABCD protocol, EARS collected smartphone foregound application-use data over a three-week sensing period, with the system querying the Android UsageStats API at 15-minute intervals and recording, for the previous 24 hours, which Apps were used in the foreground of the phone and corresponding timestamps of App opening and closing.

While ABCD contains EARS data for both Apple and Android users, the time-stamped application foreground data was only available for Android users, so our sample was confined to a subset of Android users in the ABCD cohort.

text.text: The original ACS has 20 items; here we used a short, 10-item subset of these questions, following the Affective Research Core short-form materials (University of Wisconsin-Madison; https://arc.psych.wisc.edu/self-report/attentioncontrol-scale-attc/).

As displayed in Figure S2, we found the ACS was significantly positively associated with App-journey network modularity (β = 0.289 [SE = 0.107], p = 0.008, BF10 = 5.160), but Bayes Factors indicated substantial evidence for the null hypothesis of an association between attentional control and network density (β = -0.090 [SE = 0.111], p = 0.423, BF10 = 0.305).
